I EXPECTED THIS ONE TO BREAK AND IT DID NOT. The evidence made two claims I read as tells of a fabricated trail: that a 1955 Grove Press anthology still in copyright had been read on Wikisource, and that Keene's anthology prints romanised Japanese beside the English. Both turn out to be true. The page at en.wikisource.org/wiki/Anthology_of_Japanese_Literature/Kokinshu exists, is a transcription of the Kokinshu selection of Donald Keene's Anthology of Japanese Literature, sets romaji above the English throughout (the poems before this one open Tagitsu se no, Haru tateba, Oiraku no), and carries about twenty poems from the collection with Keene's own introductory note on it.

THE WORDING IS KEENE'S AND IT MATCHES CHARACTER FOR CHARACTER. I asked that page for this poem specifically. It prints the romaji 'Hana no iro wa / Utsurinikeri na / Itazura ni / Wa ga mi yo ni furu / Nagame seshi ma ni' and under it 'The flowers withered, / Their color faded away, / While meaninglessly / I spent my days in the world / And the long rains were falling.', names Ono no Komachi as the poet and credits the translation to Donald Keene. Five lines, five lines in the proposal, in the translator's lineation with a capital at each line head, the American spelling color as printed, a full stop after falling, no straight double quote and no dash. Translation drift is the main failure mode on this track and there was room for it here, because this poem has many rival English versions in circulation, several of which turn nagame into gazing and furu into growing old: the card does not drift toward any of them, it reproduces Keene.

THE LOCATOR SURVIVES, THOUGH THE ANTHOLOGY IS NOT WHERE IT COMES FROM. The Wikisource page gives no Kokinshu number and no page number for the poem, so 'poem 113' is not read off the wording source, and the verifier was right to drop the unconfirmed page 78 rather than keep it. I checked the number independently against the Ogura Hyakunin Isshu listing, where this poem stands ninth and its source is given as Kokinshu, Spring II, 113. So the citation is sound as written: the poem is Kokinshu 113, and the English is the one printed in Keene's anthology, which is exactly what the source line says.

WHAT ELSE I TRIED AND COULD NOT MAKE STICK. (1) Misattribution. The poem is Komachi's in the Kokinshu itself and in every later anthology; she is not on the brief's trap list. (2) Speaker. A waka in the poet's own voice; no character, none owed. (3) The translator's identity inside a multi-hand anthology. Keene's anthology does use other translators for other sections, so this mattered, and the page credits this poem to Keene by name. (4) Scope. Tenth century in Japanese, 1955 in English, poetry, not scripture, film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory. (5) Publishability. The poem is about beauty fading and time spent for nothing; there is nothing graphic and nothing needing a warning. (6) Gates. shipped.js on the exact line with 'Ono no Komachi': shipped [], near [], ono no komachi at 0 of 3 for the year, not banned, not on personsAtCap, and she stands nowhere else in the month's verdicts. Source line is 99 characters and leads with her name. Tag Poetry is the form of the work.

ONE THING THE EDITOR MAY WANT, WHICH IS NOT A REFUTATION. The note is empty. This is the poem Komachi is known by and the English hides its double meaning: nagame is both the long rains and gazing in reverie, and furu is both the rain falling and the poet passing her days, which is why Keene can give both the rains and the spent days from one line. A clause saying so would earn its space and would also explain to a reader who meets another translation why the two look so different. Optional, and the line ships without it.

THEME. August is impermanence and this is the month's clearest statement of the flowers' half of it, held just short of bleak because the regret is rueful rather than despairing.
